name: Cold exposure for mood

lead: Cold exposure for mood means deliberately taking cold showers or plunging into cold water, with the aim of feeling more alert, resilient or disciplined. In looksmaxxing and self-improvement circles it is often grouped with habits that supposedly build willpower and improve energy.

Research on cold-water immersion is mostly about athletic recovery. Reviews report some reduction in perceived stress and improved sleep or quality of life after exposure, but the underlying studies are described as small and of fair to poor quality.

paras: Proponents attribute effects to the body's stress response to cold, and to the psychological act of voluntarily doing something uncomfortable. Researchers studying the Wim Hof Method have proposed that adrenaline changes may reduce inflammation, but authors of the relevant meta-analysis rated the evidence very low quality.

Medical bodies and scientists note risks of hypothermia, circulatory shock and sudden cardiac events from cold-water immersion. The American Heart Association and British Heart Foundation advise consulting a physician first. Breathing exercises combined with water immersion have been linked in reports to blackout and drowning deaths.

lead: Cold exposure for mood is the practice of using cold showers, ice baths or cold plunges in the hope of improving mood, energy and mental toughness. In looksmaxxing and wider self-improvement communities it is frequently described as a discipline habit as well as a physical one [1].

Cold-water immersion (ice bathing) is best studied as a sports recovery method. A Cochrane review cited on Wikipedia found some evidence that it reduces delayed-onset muscle soreness and perceived fatigue after exercise, with no good evidence of other benefits [1]. A 2024 meta-analysis reported an apparent decline in perceived stress within 12 hours of exposure, along with improved sleep and quality-of-life scores, though the underlying studies were fair to poor quality [1].

Health bodies warn about risks including hypothermia, circulatory shock and sudden cardiac death, and the Wim Hof Method, which pairs cold exposure with breathing exercises, has been linked in media and legal reports to a number of deaths [1][2].
infobox: Lifestyle practice (cold showers, ice baths, cold plunges)
Typical water temperature in ice baths
About 10 to 15 degrees C (50 to 59 F) [1]

paras: Ice baths, also called cold plunges or cold-water immersion, involve immersing much of the body in cold water for a short time. Athletes use them mainly after training; suggested durations in different sources range from about 5 to 20 minutes [1].

In mood-focused versions, people use cold showers or plunges as a daily habit. Wikipedia notes that ice baths are increasingly promoted for perceived mental health benefits, including relief of depression symptoms [1].

No studies found testing cold showers specifically as a looksmaxxing or appearance intervention. Related research on cold-water immersion is mostly in athletes. A Cochrane review reported some evidence for reduced soreness and perceived fatigue after exercise [1]. A 2024 meta-analysis of controlled trials, published in PLOS ONE in 2025, reported an apparent drop in perceived stress within 12 hours of exposure and improved sleep and quality-of-life scores, but rated the evidence as fair to poor [1].

For the Wim Hof Method, a 2024 meta-analysis of eight studies suggested the method may reduce inflammation, possibly through increased epinephrine; the authors judged the evidence very low quality because of small, mostly male samples and difficulty blinding participants [2].

Wikipedia reports that the medical and scientific communities broadly agree that ice baths can pose serious risks, including hypothermia, circulatory shock and sudden cardiac death, and cites research on cold shock and autonomic conflict [1].

The American Heart Association and British Heart Foundation advise consulting a physician before cold therapy [2]. Regarding the Wim Hof Method, reports describe deaths by drowning among practitioners, attributed by relatives to breathing exercises that can cause hyperventilation and fainting; one documentary linked thirteen deaths to the method [2].

Some researchers have also said that cold-water immersion right after resistance training may blunt muscle growth, though the authors called this uncertain [1]. Scientists criticised large-scale ice orders at the 2024 Paris Olympics as unproven [1].
